qs.q: A value of $k$ for which the following vectors \[ v_1=(k,0,k),\quad v_2=(2k,-3,4)\quad\text{and}\quad v_3=(3,5,2) \] are linearly dependent is
hints: Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are dependent exactly when a certain determinant vanishes.
Build the $3\times3$ matrix with the vectors as rows, compute its determinant in terms of $k$, and set it equal to zero.
$n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are linearly dependent if and only if the determinant of the matrix having them as rows (or columns) is $0$.
qs.note: k=0 also makes the vectors dependent (v1 = 0) but is not among the choices.

hints: Writing $w$ as a linear combination of given vectors leads to a linear system.
Compare components to get three equations in $a,b,c$ and solve them by elimination.
$w=av_1+bv_2+cv_3$ means the vector equation holds in each component, giving a $3\times3$ linear system for the coefficients.
steps: From the third equation $a=\dfrac{2b+8}{3}$. Substituting into the first two gives $7b+6c=11$ and $7b+9c=-1$.
qs.brief: Solve the system: $a=6,\ b=5,\ c=-4$, so $a+b-c=15$.

qs.q: Consider the subspace $S$ of $\mathbb{R}^4$ defined by $S=\{(a,b,c,d)\mid a=b+c+d\}$. A basis of $S$ is consisting of the vectors
hints: A basis must lie in the subspace, span it, and be independent.
Find the free variables of the defining condition and write a general element as a combination of vectors.
A basis of a subspace consists of linearly independent vectors that belong to it and span it; the number of vectors equals the dimension.
steps: These three vectors span $S$, lie in $S$, and are independent (each has a $1$ in a coordinate where the others have $0$).
So they form a basis of $S$.

qs.q: Let the solution space of the system \[\begin{aligned} x_1-2x_2-9x_3+7x_4&=0\\ x_1+x_2+3x_3+4x_4&=0\\ x_1+4x_2+15x_3+x_4&=0 \end{aligned}\] has all linear combinations of the two vectors $u=(1,-4,1,0)$ and $v=(\alpha,1,\beta,1)$. Then $\alpha+\beta=$
hints: Find the general solution of a homogeneous system and read off its basis vectors.
Row reduce the coefficient matrix, identify the free variables, and write the solution as a combination of vectors.
For a homogeneous system, set each free variable to $1$ in turn (others $0$) to get basis vectors of the solution space; the last two coordinates of the given vectors show which variables are free.
steps: Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3: $3x_2+12x_3-3x_4=0$ and $6x_2+24x_3-6x_4=0$, the same equation $x_2+4x_3-x_4=0$.

qs.q: The rank of the matrix \[ A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3&-9&9\\3&6&2&1&6\\2&4&1&2&3\\4&8&3&0&9\end{bmatrix} \] is
hints: The rank is the number of nonzero rows after row reduction.
Use row 1 to clear the first column below the pivot and look at what is left.
The rank of a matrix is the number of nonzero rows in its row echelon form (the number of pivots).
steps: Each of these is a multiple of $(0,0,1,-4,3)$.
Clearing the other rows with it leaves zero rows, so only two rows are nonzero.
qs.brief: After clearing column 1 the other rows are multiples of $(0,0,1,-4,3)$: rank $2$.

qs.q: The solution of the initial-value problem \[ y''-y=0,\quad y(0)=0\ \text{and}\ y'(0)=5 \] is
hints: This is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients.
Write the characteristic equation, find its roots, form the general solution, then apply both initial conditions.
For $ay''+by'+cy=0$ solve $ar^2+br+c=0$; distinct real roots $r_1,r_2$ give $y=c_1e^{r_1x}+c_2e^{r_2x}$.

qs.q: The Wronskian of the functions \[ f(x)=1,\quad g(x)=x,\quad h(x)=x^2 \] is
hints: The Wronskian is a determinant of the functions and their derivatives.
Form the $3\times3$ matrix with the functions in the first row, first derivatives in the second and second derivatives in the third.
$W(f,g,h)=\begin{vmatrix}f&g&h\\f'&g'&h'\\f''&g''&h''\end{vmatrix}$.
steps: The matrix is upper triangular, so the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries.

qs.q: The general solution of the differential equation \[ 4y''-12y'+9y=0 \] is
hints: Constant-coefficient homogeneous equation: use the characteristic equation.
Write $ar^2+br+c=0$ with the given coefficients and check whether it is a perfect square.
A repeated root $r$ of the characteristic equation gives the solutions $e^{rx}$ and $xe^{rx}$.

qs.q: The general solution of the differential equation \[ y^{(3)}+3y''-4y=0 \] is
hints: Higher-order constant-coefficient equation: use the characteristic equation and factor the cubic.
Write the characteristic polynomial and look for a small integer root, then divide it out.
A root $r$ of multiplicity $m$ gives $e^{rx},xe^{rx},\dots,x^{m-1}e^{rx}$. By the rational root test, try integer divisors of the constant term.

qs.q: The general solution of the differential equation \[ y^{(4)}+18y''+81y=0 \] is
hints: Constant-coefficient equation of order four: use the characteristic equation.
The characteristic polynomial is quadratic in $r^2$; look for a perfect square.
Complex roots $a\pm bi$ of multiplicity $m$ give $x^je^{ax}\cos bx$ and $x^je^{ax}\sin bx$ for $j=0,\dots,m-1$.

qs.q: A linear homogeneous constant-coefficient differential equation which has the general solution \[ y(x)=e^{-4x}\left(c_1\cos(3x)+c_2\sin(3x)\right) \] is
hints: Work backwards from the solution to the characteristic equation.
Read off the complex roots from the exponential and trigonometric factors and build the quadratic with those roots.
Roots $a\pm bi$ correspond to $e^{ax}(c_1\cos bx+c_2\sin bx)$, and the quadratic with these roots is $(r-a)^2+b^2=0$.
steps: The solution corresponds to the roots $r=-4\pm3i$.

qs.q: If $y_p=A+Bx$ is a particular solution of the differential equation \[ y''-y'-2y=3x+4, \] then $4A+4B=$
hints: Substitute the trial solution into the equation and compare coefficients.
Compute $y_p'$ and $y_p''$, plug them in, and match the coefficients of $x$ and the constants on both sides.
Two polynomials are equal for all $x$ exactly when their coefficients of each power of $x$ agree.

qs.q: An appropriate form of a particular solution $y_p$ for the non-homogeneous differential equation $y''+4y=3x\cos(2x)$ is given by $y_p(x)=$
hints: Use undetermined coefficients and check whether the trial form overlaps the complementary solution.
Find the complementary solution of the homogeneous equation and compare it with the natural trial form.
If a term of the trial function solves the homogeneous equation, multiply the whole trial function by $x^s$ with the smallest $s$ that removes the overlap.
steps: The natural trial form for $3x\cos2x$ is $(A+Bx)\cos2x+(C+Dx)\sin2x$, which overlaps $y_c$.
qs.brief: $y_c$ has $\cos2x,\sin2x$, so multiply the trial form by $x$: $(Ax+Bx^2)\cos2x+(Cx+Dx^2)\sin2x$.

qs.q: Given that $y_p=u_1(x)\cos(3x)+u_2(x)\sin(3x)$ is a particular solution of the differential equation \[ y''+9y=2\sec(3x), \] then $u_1(x)=$
hints: This is variation of parameters.
Take $y_1=\cos3x$, $y_2=\sin3x$, compute their Wronskian, and then the formula for $u_1'$.
For $y''+Py'+Qy=f$: $u_1'=-\dfrac{y_2f}{W}$, $u_2'=\dfrac{y_1f}{W}$ with $W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2$; also $\int\tan(kx)\,dx=-\dfrac1k\ln|\cos kx|$.

qs.q: The characteristic polynomial of the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}3&5&-2\\0&2&0\\0&2&1\end{bmatrix}$ is $p(\lambda)=$
hints: The characteristic polynomial comes from a determinant involving $\lambda$.
Form $A-\lambda I$ and expand its determinant along a column with many zeros.
$p(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I)$ (note the sign convention: the leading term is $(-\lambda)^n$).

qs.q: The eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}7&-8\\6&-7\end{bmatrix}$ is $\begin{bmatrix}a\\1\end{bmatrix}$, where $a=$
hints: Eigenvectors for $\lambda$ are the nonzero solutions of a homogeneous system.
Form $A-\lambda I$ for the given eigenvalue and solve $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v}=(a,1)$.
An eigenvector $\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}$ of eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$.

qs.q: If the characteristic polynomial of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}5&-6&3\\6&-7&3\\6&-6&2\end{bmatrix}$ is $p(\lambda)=-(\lambda+1)^2(\lambda-2)$, then a basis for the eigenspace of $\lambda=-1$ is $v_1=\begin{bmatrix}m\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}$ and $v_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\n\end{bmatrix}$, where $m+n=$
hints: The eigenspace is the null space of $A-\lambda I$.
Form $A+I$, reduce it, and require each given vector to satisfy the resulting equation.
The eigenspace of $\lambda$ is the solution space of $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$.
steps: $A+I=\begin{bmatrix}6&-6&3\\6&-6&3\\6&-6&3\end{bmatrix}$, which reduces to the single equation $2x-2y+z=0$.

qs.q: If the rank of the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\1&5&-9\\2&5&m\end{bmatrix}$ is equal to $2$, then $m=$
hints: Rank less than $3$ for a square matrix means the matrix is singular.
Set the determinant of the matrix equal to zero and solve for $m$, then check the rank is exactly $2$.
A $3\times3$ matrix has rank less than $3$ if and only if its determinant is $0$.
steps: Expand the determinant along the first row: $1(5m+45)-2(m+18)+3(5-10)$.
Then the first two rows are independent, so the rank is exactly $2$.

qs.q: Which one of the following set of functions are linearly dependent
hints: Look for a set where one function is a combination of the others.
Check each set for a relation, or compute the Wronskian; a nonzero Wronskian at some point proves independence.
Functions are linearly dependent if some nontrivial combination $c_1y_1+c_2y_2+c_3y_3$ is identically zero; if $W\neq0$ at some point they are independent.
steps: In the first set $y_3=2x+3=2y_2+3y_1$, so $3y_1+2y_2-y_3=0$: dependent.
In each other set the highest powers of $x$ occur in only one function (or the Wronskian is nonzero), so no nontrivial combination vanishes.
So the first set is the linearly dependent one.
qs.brief: $2x+3=2\cdot x+3\cdot1$, so $\{1,x,2x+3\}$ is dependent; the others are independent.

qs.q: If the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}5&-3\\2&0\end{bmatrix}$ is diagonalizable with a diagonalizing matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $P^{-1}AP=D$, then
hints: Diagonalization uses eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Find the eigenvalues, then an eigenvector for each; make sure the columns of $P$ appear in the same order as the eigenvalues in $D$.
If $A\mathbf{v}_i=\lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i$, then $P=[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ satisfy $P^{-1}AP=D$.
